GET TO KNOW YOUR SOUND

Treble, explained.

Treble changes brightness using a high-shelf filter. It raises or lowers a broad region above a transition frequency, affecting cymbals, vocal detail and hiss. A negative gain softens the recording; a positive gain brightens it.

Understand the parametersFind your starting pointWhat to listen forCommon question

Every parameter, explained

Treble gain

-18 dB to 24 dB · Default -18 dB

Treble gain ranges from −18 to +24 dB. The default −18 dB is a strong cut, not a boost. Use 0 dB for a neutral comparison or raise above zero to add brightness.

Frequency

1000 Hz to 10000 Hz · Default 1000 Hz

Frequency sets the shelf transition between 1 kHz and 10 kHz. At the default 1 kHz, the change reaches upper mids as well as highs. At 6–10 kHz it focuses more on sparkle and hiss.

A good place to start

Try −6 dB at 6 kHz to soften an edgy mix, or +3 dB at 6 kHz for a little extra detail. The default −18 dB at 1 kHz deliberately produces a much darker result.

What to listen for

Boosting can make hiss and harsh vocal consonants more obvious. Cutting too low can dull intelligibility. Overall peak protection can lower output after a strong boost, so compare tonal balance rather than assuming higher gain means higher total loudness.

Is this noise removal?

No. A treble cut also reduces wanted high-frequency detail. It does not distinguish noise from instruments or voice.

Make a version you want to keep

Upload your audio or try the sample, adjust the controls above, then click Apply effects. Select Original and Result to compare. Change the settings and apply again to revise. Every revision starts from the untouched original, and Download WAV saves the latest applied version. The player’s Volume control changes only listening volume.

WELCOME TO SONIC

Your sound, in three steps.

  1. Bring your audio.

    Upload a supported file, or listen to the built-in sample.

  2. Explore your effects.

    Selecting an effect includes it automatically. Adjust its settings or remove it from the chain.

  3. Listen and experiment.

    Click Apply effects, compare Original and Result, adjust and apply again, then download your WAV. Tempo preserves pitch; pitch shift preserves duration.
